What to choose
- Front-clip no-pull harness (primary recommendation): the leash attaches at the chest so you get immediate lateral steering that discourages forward lunges. Good for steady, humane control while you train loose-leash walking.
- Head-collar (Gentle Leader / Halti): very effective at stopping pullers because it controls the head, but many dogs need slow, positive acclimation. Use only with training and supervision.
- Dual-attachment harness (front + back): gives flexibility — use the front clip for training/walks and the back clip for relaxed outings or car travel.
- Avoid relying on back-clip only harnesses if strong pulling is the main problem — they don’t give good steering and can encourage pulling.

Fit checklist (do this every time you put it on)
1. Measure first: the most important measurement is girth (widest part of the ribcage, just behind the front legs). Also note neck circumference. Bring those when you shop.
2. Snug but not tight: you should be able to fit two fingers between strap and dog. Straps that ride up toward the throat will cause rubbing or pressure.
3. Chest strap placement: the front clip should sit low on the sternum (not high on the throat). The straps should not press on the trachea.
4. No chafing: choose padded straps or add a soft liner if you see rubbing under the armpits.
5. Escape-proofing: if Marzipan tries to back out, pick a harness with a neck strap plus belly strap and a secure buckle layout (some designs have two buckles).

Training and handling tips
- Use a 4–6 foot flat leash (no retractables). Shorten up when you’re actively training.
- Reward loose-leash walking immediately with high-value treats and calm praise. Click or mark when she’s by your side.
- Stop-and-start: when she pulls, stop walking, wait for slack, then continue. Change direction occasionally so she learns to pay attention to you.
- Combine harness with cue training (e.g., “let’s go”) and frequent rewards. For very stubborn pulling, a head-collar for short periods can accelerate progress while you train.
- If she’s reactive or very strong, consider a session or two with a positive-reinforcement trainer to set up a plan.

Specific models commonly recommended (examples to look at)

- Ruffwear Front Range or Front-Range-style harnesses (front + back clip, good fit and padding).
